transcript.content: Hello. What brings you into the clinic today?

In longer work meetings I just can’t stay in my seat—I keep getting up to move around even when I know it looks unprofessional. It has started to affect how my colleagues and managers view me, so I wanted to get some help to figure out why this is happening.
Have you experienced this kind of restlessness and difficulty staying still since childhood, or is this something that started more recently in your adult life?

It definitely goes back to my childhood; even in elementary school, teachers always complained to my parents that I couldn't stay in my seat and would walk around the classroom. It just never caused major problems until about two years ago, when my new role started requiring me to sit through long, structured meetings instead of doing hands-on coding.
Do you often experience persistent, excessive worry about various everyday things like work, health, or family, or is your restlessness mainly a physical urge to move?

It is definitely almost entirely a physical urge to move rather than mental anxiety or worrying about everyday things. Whenever I have to sit still for more than half an hour, I get this pent-up, jittery feeling in my body, like I need to stretch or walk around or I'm going to crawl out of my skin.
Besides the physical restlessness, do you also struggle with things like sustaining your attention on tasks, staying organized, or frequently forgetting daily details?

Yes, absolutely. During Zoom calls, my mind often drifts off after about ten minutes and I miss chunks of what was discussed, and trying to organize my weekly tasks feels so overwhelming that I just end up bouncing between them. I also tend to get sidetracked easily and forget to finish the final steps of a project, like updating a Jira ticket, even if I started the work enthusiastically.
Do you notice these difficulties with focus and restlessness affecting other areas of your life outside of work, such as at home or in your personal relationships?

Yes, it definitely spills over into my personal life as well. For instance, during my kids' school assemblies, I get that intense, jittery feeling where I feel like I'm going to crawl out of my skin if I have to sit still. I also notice I get really impatient and antsy just waiting in everyday lines, like at the coffee shop.
Do you also find yourself frequently interrupting others during conversations, or struggling to wait your turn to speak?

Yes, I definitely do. In one-on-ones I constantly jump in with solutions or finish my engineers' sentences because my brain is racing ahead and I feel this urge to say it right away. I also get really impatient and antsy waiting my turn to speak in larger group meetings, and I find myself feeling annoyed that everything is moving so slowly.
Have these challenges with attention and restlessness been constant throughout your life, or do they seem to come and go in distinct phases or episodes?

They have definitely been a constant presence throughout my life rather than coming in episodes. Even back in elementary school, teachers complained about me walking around the classroom, blurting out answers, and not staying in my seat. It has always been there, but it only became a major problem about two years ago when my new job role started requiring these long, structured meetings.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets the criteria for ICD-10 F90.0 (Disturbance of activity and attention / ADHD, combined presentation). He exhibits a persistent pattern of both inattention (mind drifting during meetings, organization difficulties, failing to complete final steps of tasks) and hyperactivity/impulsivity (inability to remain seated, subjective physical restlessness, interrupting others, impatience) that has been present since childhood. These symptoms cause significant functional impairment across multiple settings (work and personal life). Generalized Anxiety Disorder (F41.1) was considered due to the restlessness, but was ruled out as the patient confirmed the symptoms are physical urges rather than driven by excessive worry or mental anxiety.
